title: Good and Bad: bene- and mal-
short: bene- means well and mal- means badly.
trouble: Not every word that starts with ben- or mal- has these parts: bench and mall do not.

blocks.html: Two small Latin parts sort a whole family of words into good and bad. bene- means “well” (you know it from benefit) and mal- means “badly” (you know it from malfunction: something that works badly). Put one in front of the same root and the meaning flips.

blocks.name: vo-scene

scene.alt: A smiling boy offers a gift, labeled bene, while a caped trickster sneaks by, labeled mal.

blocks.cap: A smiling boy offers a gift, labeled bene, while a caped trickster sneaks by, labeled mal.

blocks.html: bene- = well, good. mal- (also male-) = badly, bad. A bene- word points to kindness or help; a mal- word points to harm, illness or trouble.

The clearest pair is benevolent and malevolent. Both end in vol (wish, will, as in volunteer). A benevolent person wishes others well; a malevolent one wishes them harm. Watch for the same trick in other pairs: benefactor (one who does good) and malefactor (one who does wrong).

head: Word and meaning
Parts, and what they say
rows:
benefactor
a person who gives money or help to a person or cause

beneficiary
a person who receives a benefit, such as money left in a will

bene well + fic do + -iary one who
→ “one who is done good (who receives)”

malcontent
a person who is always dissatisfied and complaining
blocks.cap: Each word, what it means now, and its parts. Words in italics are familiar words that are not on the list.

blocks.title: Giver or receiver?
blocks.q: Grandpa’s will left his telescope to Kai. Is Kai the benefactor or the beneficiary?
steps: Both start with bene- (well), so both have to do with good done.
benefactor ends in -or, “one who”: the one who does good, the giver.
beneficiary names the one who is done good to: the receiver.
blocks.a: Kai is the beneficiary; Grandpa was the benefactor.

blocks.name: vo-word

entry.def: kind and wishing good for others
entry.ex: The {benevolent} neighbor shoveled every driveway on the street after the storm.
entry.ctx: Though the old shopkeeper looked stern, the town knew him to be {benevolent}; every winter he quietly paid the heating bills of families who could not.
entry.etym: From Latin benevolens, “wishing well”: bene (well) + volens (wishing).

mn.text: Every Saturday, Ben volunteers at the bread table; a man who gives his time to help others is {benevolent}.

scene.alt: Ben, in an apron, hands out free bread to happy children.

blocks.cap: A word from the list: benevolent.

blocks.name: vo-word

entry.def: an illness, or a deep-rooted problem
entry.ex: Boredom is a common {malady} on long car trips.
entry.ctx: The town’s real {malady} was not its empty storefronts but its loss of hope; once neighbors began working together, the shops slowly filled again.
entry.etym: From Old French maladie, from malade, “sick,” from Latin male habitus, “in poor condition.”

mn.text: Poor Granny Mae is the lady with the bad cold; her {malady} keeps her in bed.

scene.alt: An old lady lies in bed with a bad cold, sneezing.

blocks.cap: A word from the list: malady.

blocks.html: Not every word that starts with ben or mal has these parts. A bench and a mall have nothing to do with good or bad, and the word male comes from a different Latin word. Check that the rest of the word makes sense with “well” or “badly” in front of it.
